claim: 1a. Small home-services businesses (about $1-1.5M EBITDA) trade near 3 to 4.5x EBITDA.
correct: Broadly right as a median, low versus some advisers. Axial HVAC transaction data: median 4.48x for $1-3M EBITDA (range 2.58-7.69x); 3.12x under $1M. Adastra Equity (updated Jun 5, 2026, built on Capstone and GF Data samples) puts $1-3M EBITDA at 5.0-7.0x and reserves 3.0-4.5x for under $1M. Kroll (Nov 4, 2025): small founder-owned tuck-ins trade at 3 to 8x. Use 3.5-5x as the base case for a $1-1.5M owner-run shop.

claim: 1b. Platforms at $2.5-3M+ EBITDA with professional management sell to PE-backed consolidators at 7 to 8x.
correct: 7-8x is the upper range at that size, not the median. Axial medians: 5.88x for $3-5M EBITDA, 7.02x only at $5M+. Adastra: 5.0-7.0x for $1-3M, 7.0-10.0x for $3-10M. Kroll: 'platform' multiples (mid-teens) apply to much larger high-quality businesses; professionalized add-ons can reach 8x. GF Data 2025 average across PE-backed deals ($1M-$500M TEV) was 7.2x, with only a 3% premium for above-average performers. Plan the exit at about 6x for $2.5-3M EBITDA and treat 7-8x as upside, or plan to reach $5M+ EBITDA.

claim: 2a. Most Rhode Island HVAC shops quote hourly.
correct: No survey of Rhode Island (or national) contractor pricing method was found. Treat it as a diligence question for each target, not a market fact.

claim: 2b. Flat-rate pricing (ServiceTitan pricebook) and membership plans lift price.
correct: Directionally supported by vendor data only: ServiceTitan (May 12, 2020; 179 clients) found Pricebook Pro users' average ticket grew 14% YoY vs 8% for non-users, about $34 higher. Vendor case studies (e.g., Jake's Heating & Cooling: average ticket up 27%, gross profit up 10%) are self-selected. No independent study isolates the effect of membership plans on price.

claim: 2c. A 5% price lift on $6-8M revenue is $300-400k, mostly to EBITDA.
correct: Arithmetic is right: 5% x $6M = $300k; 5% x $8M = $400k. 'Mostly to EBITDA' holds only if volume holds: a pure price increase has no added parts or labor cost, so the flow-through is close to 100% minus commissions and spiffs paid on revenue (often a few points), card or financing fees, and any lost jobs. Member discounts on repairs also offset part of the lift. Model 70-90% flow-through, i.e. $210-360k.
source: Arithmetic; flow-through range is analyst judgment, not sourced. Price-effect evidence: https://www.servicetitan.com/coronavirus/pricebook-pro-users-seeing-stronger-ticket-sizes-in-2020

claim: 3a. Rhode Island has a 'Clean Heat Standard' or equivalent law pulling demand toward heat pumps.
correct: No Clean Heat Standard is law in Rhode Island as of Nov 2026. H7912 (Rhode Island Clean Heat Standard Act, sponsor Cortvriend, introduced Feb 27, 2026; tradeable clean heat credits, DEM rules, compliance from July 1, 2028) was held for further study in House Environment and Natural Resources on Mar 25, 2026. OER, the Division of Public Utilities and Carriers and DEM jointly opposed it in writing ('it would increase heating costs'). Earlier versions (H5167 / S0407, 2025) also did not pass.

claim: 3b. Mass Save is Massachusetts's program; what Rhode Island's actual programs are (Rhode Island Energy rebates, Clean Heat RI, Act on Climate 2021).
correct: Mass Save is Massachusetts only. Rhode Island has: (1) Act on Climate (2021): enforceable mandates of 45% below 1990 by 2030, 80% by 2040, net zero by 2050; 2025 Climate Action Strategy on a five-year cycle. It sets targets but does not itself mandate heat pumps. (2) Rhode Island Energy rebates (2026 rules from Jan 1, 2026): $1,500/ton enhanced rebate for electric-baseboard customers (participating contractor required), up to $625/ton standard rebate for gas, oil, propane or electric customers; equipment must meet ENERGY STAR 6.1 cold-climate criteria; R-410A systems no longer qualify. (3) Clean Heat Rhode Island (OER, state): income-eligible households (<150% state median income) get 60% of project up to $11,500 via its Heat Pump Installer Network; over 4,900 installs to date. (4) New England Heat Pump Accelerator (announced Mar 27, 2026): $35M federally funded, $650/unit air-source and $300/unit heat pump water heater midstream incentives at distributors, through Dec 2029. Being in the Clean Heat RI installer network and RI Energy participating-contractor lists is a real channel to target.

claim: 4a. Federal set-aside goal for SDVOSBs is 3%.
correct: The government-wide SDVOSB prime contracting goal was raised from 3% to 5% by Section 863 of the FY2024 NDAA (P.L. 118-31, enacted Dec 22, 2023). Awards count toward the goal only if made to SBA-certified firms (Sec. 864); SBA ended goal credit for self-certified SDVOSBs effective Aug 5, 2024. Certification moved from VA to SBA under the FY2021 NDAA. (Rhode Island's own state procurement goal for veteran-owned small businesses is 'no less than 3%' under R.I. Gen. Laws 37-14.3-4, which may be the source of the 3% figure.)

claim: 4b. VA's Vets First gives SDVOSBs priority.
correct: 38 U.S.C. 8127/8128 (VAAR 819.70): VA must set aside to SDVOSBs (then VOSBs) when two or more capable verified firms are expected to offer at a fair price (Rule of Two, 8127(d)); Kingdomware (2016) made it apply to FSS and other orders. VA sole-source authority to a single SDVOSB or VOSB is up to $5M under 8127(b)/(c) with a written J&A. Only applies to VA buys (e.g., Providence VA Medical Center), not to Navy or Guard work. The VA FAQ still refers to the old VIP database; certification is now through SBA.

claim: 4c. Naval Station Newport contracts mechanical work through SDVOSB set-asides.
correct: At least sometimes. NUWC Division Newport solicitation N66604-25-R-0046 'HVAC Maintenance and Repair' at Naval Station Newport (posted Oct 10, 2024; NAICS 238220, $19M size standard) was an SDVOSB set-aside. NAVFAC Mid-Atlantic's Newport HVAC preventive maintenance IDC sources-sought (N4008524R2529, Jan 2024; 60 months; capability threshold of at least $900k per year) was issued without a set-aside decision. So set-asides exist but are decided per requirement; larger base-wide maintenance contracts may go to other socioeconomic categories or full and open.

claim: 4d. Quonset (Quonset Business Park, RI Air National Guard) contracts mechanical work through SDVOSB set-asides.
correct: No SDVOSB set-aside for mechanical work at Quonset or the 143rd Airlift Wing was found. Quonset Business Park itself is run by the state's Quonset Development Corporation (not sourced here), so federal set-aside rules would not govern its own work. Rhode Island National Guard facility HVAC work found (Camp Fogarty Armory HVAC Replacement, RFQ25005691, 2025) was a state-level procurement with no set-aside stated. Air Guard construction elsewhere is set aside to SDVOSBs through USPFO offices (e.g., Virginia ANG W50S9B26BA003, Sep 2026, $1-5M), so it is possible but unproven for Quonset.

claim: 4e. FAR sole-source limits for SDVOSBs (2026 dollar thresholds).
correct: FAR 19.1406(a)(2) (FAC 2026-01, effective Mar 13, 2026): up to $8.5M including options for manufacturing NAICS codes and $5M for all other NAICS codes (HVAC service, NAICS 238220, falls under $5M). Conditions: no reasonable expectation of two or more SDVOSB offers, responsible firm, fair and reasonable price, not already in 8(a). Since Jan 1, 2024 the firm must be SBA-certified (or have applied by Dec 31, 2023). Related Oct 1, 2025 inflation changes: micro-purchase $15,000, simplified acquisition threshold $350,000.

claim: 5. Dispatch optimization, GPS routing and a parts runner add 1 to 2 billable hours per tech per day.
correct: Benchmark: Field Promax (via ACHR News, Jul 21, 2026) finds about 5.7 billable hours in an 8.8-hour day (65%), with about 1.13 hours of unrecovered driving. FieldEdge (Jun 2026) calls 70-85% utilization healthy (5.6-6.8 of 8 hours) and its own routing example is 30 minutes per tech per day. Moving from 65% to 80% of 8.8 hours is about 1.3 hours, so +1 hour is a stretch target for a poorly run shop; +2 hours would exceed the healthy band. Use +0.5 to 1.0 hour as the base case.

claim: 6. Consolidating to one distributor (Ferguson, Winsupply) earns rebates; typical rebate levels.
correct: No published typical distributor-to-contractor rebate rate was found. Published rebate research covers manufacturer-to-distributor rebates (rebates are 40-70% of many HVAC distributors' net profit, hvacrtrends Dec 30, 2025). Ferguson's contractor program (PRO Plus) is points-based (1 point per dollar spent online, 2-4x on promoted items) with no stated cash value. Contractor savings from consolidation come mainly from negotiated net pricing and manufacturer contractor programs, which must be quoted per account.

claim: 7. Card-on-file and consumer financing (Service Finance, GreenSky) cut receivables from 45 days to near zero, freeing $400-700k on $7M revenue.
correct: Arithmetic: 45 days x $7M / 365 = $863k of receivables. Taking all of it to about 5 days frees about $767k; the claimed $400-700k equals cutting DSO by 21-37 days. Benchmarks (Level, undated, method not disclosed): residential and light-commercial HVAC service 30-45 days; commercial mechanical 60-75 days. Card-on-file and consumer financing work for residential jobs only; commercial accounts will stay on terms. Right range: about $(residential share x $863k); e.g. 50-80% residential gives roughly $430-690k. Cost offsets: consumer financing dealer fees run 0-2.75% for standard installment loans but 11.5-18.5% for true 0% APR plans (GreenSky rate sheet, Sep 2022), and card fees apply to card-on-file. Freed cash is one-time, not recurring EBITDA.

claim: 8a. SBA 7(a): maximum loan $5M.
correct: $5 million for most 7(a) loans ($500k for SBA Express). Guarantee 75% on loans over $350k. Term generally up to 10 years for business acquisition without real estate.

claim: 8b. Typical equity injection 10%; seller notes on standby count toward equity.
correct: Under SOP 50 10 8 (effective Jun 1, 2025) a complete change of ownership needs at least 10% equity, measured on all costs of the change. A seller note counts only if on full standby (no payments) for the entire life of the SBA loan (SBA Form 155) and only up to half the required injection, i.e. 5% of project cost; the buyer must bring at least 5% in cash or other eligible equity. The earlier 24-month standby rule no longer applies.

claim: 8c. Current rates: prime plus spread, 2026.
correct: WSJ prime was 7.00% as of Oct 30, 2026 (also 7.00% a year earlier, per Bankrate). SBA maximum variable spread for loans over $350k is prime + 3.0%, so the cap is 10.00% today.

claim: 8d. With SBA 7(a) at 90%, a 10% EBITDA improvement is roughly a 30%+ equity value swing.
correct: Understated at entry, right only after about 3 years of paydown. Example: $1.3M EBITDA x 3.5x = $4.55M EV; 90% loan = $4.095M at 10.0% (prime 7.00 + 3.00), 10-year amortization ($649k per year debt service); equity $455k. At a constant multiple, +10% EBITDA = +$455k EV = +100% of entry equity. After 3 years the balance is about $3.26M, equity about $1.29M, so the swing is about 35%. After 5 years: balance $2.55M, equity $2.00M, swing about 23%. After 7 years: about 16%. (Assumes constant EBITDA and multiple, no cash build-up, fees or working capital; with a 5% standby seller note, the buyer's cash is only $228k, so the swing on cash invested at entry is about 200%.) The same leverage works in reverse: a 10% EBITDA drop at entry wipes out all equity.

claim: 9. Hiring a GM is a condition for the exit multiple step-up (owner-dependence discount in lower middle market valuations).
correct: Supported by adviser sources rather than a rigorous study: Adastra Equity (Jun 5, 2026) says an owner who is the main rainmaker is priced 1.0-2.0x EBITDA below the industry average and owner-replaceable businesses trade 1.0-2.0x above owner-dependent peers; it cites 30-50% value reductions for fully owner-dependent businesses (Bennett Financials, Succession Thinking) and First Page Sage data that about 52% of listed HVAC businesses do not sell, mainly due to owner dependence and customer attrition. Axial lists owner dependence as a value reducer. Kroll notes founders often stay on with earnouts, which is how buyers price owner risk. A GM is necessary but not sufficient: the step-up also needs size (Axial medians rise mainly with EBITDA band).
